rows.query: Compare Buffett's stated holding horizon for Coca-Cola in 1988 with the cash-dividend outcome reported in 2022: how long did he favor holding outstanding businesses, and what dividends did Coke pay Berkshire in 1994 and 2022?
rows.answer: The cash dividend we received from Coke in 1994 was $75 million. [1] We care not whether the auditors hear a tree fall in the forest. [2] we do care who owns the tree. [2] what's next done with it. [2] When Coca-Cola uses retained earnings to repurchase its shares, the company increases our percentage ownership in what I regard to be the most valuable franchise in the world. [2] (Coke also, of course, uses retained earnings in many other value-enhancing ways.) Instead of repurchasing stock, Coca-Cola could pay those funds to us in dividends, which we could then use to purchase more Coke shares. [2] That would be a less efficient scenario: Because of taxes we would pay on dividend income, we would not be able to increase our proportionate ownership to the degree that Coke can, acting for us. [2] If this less efficient procedure were followed, however, Berkshire would report far greater "earnings." I believe the best way to think about our earnings is in terms of "look-through" results, calculated as follows: Take $250 million, which is roughly our share of the 1990 operating earnings retained by our investees. [2] subtract $30 million, for the incremental taxes we would have owed had that $250 million been paid to us in dividends. [2] add the remainder, $220 million, to our reported operating earnings of $371 million. [2]
